title: What AI can learn from brains, and what brains can learn from AI
text:
15_02  WHAT AI CAN LEARN FROM BRAINS, AND WHAT BRAINS CAN LEARN FROM AI

The previous section showed that neuroscience and AI share a history. This section asks a forward-looking question in both directions. What properties of brains do current AI systems still lack, and could neuroscience help supply them? And what has AI already taught neuroscience, as a source of models, tools and concepts? The honest answer to both questions is mixed: there are real lessons, there are tempting analogies that mislead, and there is active disagreement among serious researchers. The aim here is to lay out the arguments, not to settle them.

PART ONE: WHAT BRAINS STILL DO BETTER

Several capabilities that brains have, and that AI systems lack or achieve only at great cost, are widely discussed.

1. Data efficiency. A child learns many words from relatively few exposures, and an animal can learn to avoid a food after one bad experience. Large language models are trained on far more text than any human could read in many lifetimes. Part of the difference may be that humans learn from rich, multimodal, interactive experience, and part may be that brains start with much more structure.

Anthony Zador argued in Nature Communications in 2019, in "A critique of pure learning and what artificial neural networks can learn from animal brains", that much of animal behaviour is not learned from scratch but encoded in the genome, which specifies wiring rules rather than individual weights. Because the genome has far too little information to specify every synapse, it must compress wiring into developmental rules, a "genomic bottleneck". Zador suggested that this bottleneck acts as a regulariser and that evolution's search over wiring rules is analogous to architecture search, with learning in each lifetime fine-tuning. For AI, the lesson would be to invest more in innate structure, inductive biases, and compressed representations of networks. Chapter 11's critical periods and Chapter 12's connectomes, with their conserved cell types, provide concrete examples of such structure.

2. Continual learning without catastrophic forgetting. Brains learn throughout life, and learning a new skill rarely erases an old one. Neural networks trained sequentially tend to overwrite earlier knowledge (Chapter 11). Neuroscience-inspired remedies include consolidating important synapses (elastic weight consolidation, inspired by synaptic consolidation), replaying old experiences (inspired by hippocampal replay and complementary learning systems theory), and sparse, modular representations. These help but do not fully solve the problem.

3. Energy efficiency. The brain runs on about 20 watts. Chapter 13_04 discussed how sparse spiking, co-located memory and computation, and analogue physics contribute, and how far neuromorphic hardware has come.

4. Robustness and generalisation. Image classifiers can be fooled by adversarial perturbations imperceptible to humans, and can rely on textures or backgrounds rather than shapes. Robert Geirhos and colleagues reported in 2019 that standard ImageNet CNNs are biased toward texture, while humans are biased toward shape. Some studies found that models whose early layers better match primate V1 are more robust to certain perturbations; for example, Joel Dapello, James DiCarlo and colleagues reported in 2020 that adding a fixed front end modelled on V1 improved adversarial robustness. Such results are suggestive, but robustness remains an open problem with many contributing factors.

5. Embodiment and active learning. Animals learn by acting: moving their eyes, touching, experimenting. Their learning is grounded in sensorimotor loops (Chapter 13_03's active inference is one theory of this). Robotics, a mechatronics student's home ground, remains far harder for AI than language, which some researchers describe as Moravec's paradox: abilities that seem easy for humans, like perception and movement, have been hard for machines, while abilities that seem hard, like chess, have been comparatively easy.

6. Learning rules. The brain apparently learns without exact backpropagation. If it uses local rules, three-factor plasticity, dendritic error signals or predictive coding (Chapters 7 and 13), these might be more suitable for neuromorphic hardware and online learning than backpropagation through time. Timothy Lillicrap and colleagues reported in 2016 that "feedback alignment", using fixed random feedback weights instead of the transposed forward weights, still allows deep networks to learn, because the forward weights come to align with the feedback. In 2020 Lillicrap, Adam Santoro, Luke Marris, Colin Akerman and Hinton reviewed evidence in Nature Reviews Neuroscience that the brain might approximate backpropagation using differences in neural activity to represent errors. Whether biologically plausible rules can match backpropagation at scale remains an open question.

7. Diverse units and neuromodulation. Brains contain many cell types (Chapter 12), multiple neurotransmitters and neuromodulators that change circuit function on the fly (Chapter 6), dendritic computation (Chapter 13_02), and glial cells whose computational roles are still debated. Standard AI networks use one unit type. Whether this diversity confers computational advantages or reflects biological constraints is not settled.

Demis Hassabis, Dharshan Kumaran, Christopher Summerfield and Matthew Botvinick argued in Neuron in 2017 that neuroscience had provided and would continue to provide inspiration for AI, pointing to attention, episodic memory, working memory and continual learning. A 2023 perspective in Nature Communications by Zador and many co-authors proposed an "embodied Turing test" as a goal for "NeuroAI": building AI systems that can interact with the world as flexibly as animals.

A COUNTERPOINT

Skeptics note that the most successful recent advances, such as transformers and large-scale self-supervised training, were not directly inspired by neuroscience. Aircraft did not need to flap their wings: an engineer can copy the principles of flight (aerodynamic lift) rather than the mechanism (feathers). Some researchers argue that AI should borrow principles, such as sparse coding, prediction, and replay, but not necessarily mechanisms, and that the mechanisms may be adaptations to biological constraints, such as slow, noisy components and metabolic cost, that silicon does not share. This argument has force: the brain is a solution to biology's problems, not necessarily the optimal solution for computing hardware. But it cuts both ways, because energy and data efficiency are now pressing constraints for AI too.

PART TWO: WHAT AI HAS TAUGHT NEUROSCIENCE

The reverse direction has been at least as productive in recent years.

1. Models that perform the task. Before deep learning, models of high-level vision or language in the brain could not actually perform realistic tasks. Task-optimised deep networks (Chapter 8) changed this, giving image-computable models of the ventral stream that predict neural responses. Blake Richards and many co-authors argued in Nature Neuroscience in 2019, in "A deep learning framework for neuroscience", that neuroscientists should describe brains as deep learning researchers describe networks: in terms of objective functions, learning rules and architectures, rather than trying to explain the function of each neuron individually. This "optimisation-based" view treats the brain as the product of optimisation and asks what it was optimised for.

2. Benchmarks for model-brain comparison. Brain-Score, developed by Martin Schrimpf, DiCarlo and colleagues, compares many artificial networks against neural and behavioural data from primate vision, producing a leaderboard. Similar efforts compare language models to human brain recordings during reading and listening. Several groups reported in the early 2020s that activations of language models predict fMRI and electrocorticography responses to language, and that models that better predict the next word also tend to better predict brain responses, though the interpretation of these correlations remains debated.

3. Tools for analysing neural data. Chapter 12 described deep learning in connectomics, calcium imaging analysis, and pose estimation (for example DeepLabCut, from the Mathis laboratories, which tracks animal body parts in video using transfer learning). Latent variable models such as LFADS and CEBRA (reported by Steffen Schneider, Jin Hwa Lee and Mackenzie Mathis in Nature in 2023) learn joint embeddings of neural activity and behaviour. These tools make experiments possible that would otherwise be infeasible.

4. Concepts. Reinforcement learning gave neuroscience the temporal-difference error as a precise hypothesis for dopamine (Chapter 6). More recently, Will Dabney, Zeb Kurth-Nelson, Naoshige Uchida and colleagues at DeepMind and Harvard reported in Nature in 2020 that dopamine neurons appear to encode a distribution of reward predictions, consistent with distributional reinforcement learning, an idea that came from AI research. The transformer's attention has prompted new models of hippocampal function (Chapter 9). Ideas from representation learning, such as disentanglement and the geometry of representations, are now standard in analysing population activity.

5. Model systems for interpretability. Artificial networks are "model organisms" in which every weight and activation can be measured and manipulated. Methods developed for neuroscience, such as representational similarity analysis, ablation, and tuning curves, are used to study networks; methods developed for networks, such as attribution, causal interventions, and sparse dictionary learning of features, are being brought back to neuroscience. Eric Jonas and Konrad Kording published a widely discussed 2017 paper, "Could a neuroscientist understand a microprocessor?", applying standard neuroscience analyses to a simulated MOS 6502 chip and finding that they revealed little about how it actually worked. It was a warning that the methods themselves need testing on systems we understand.

CAUTIONS ON BOTH SIDES

Several cautions recur in this literature.

Predicting neural data is not the same as explaining it. A deep network that predicts neuronal responses well may still be as hard to understand as the brain itself.

Similarity can be superficial. Two systems with very different mechanisms can produce similar representations if they solve similar tasks on similar data. Representational similarity alone does not prove a shared algorithm.

Metaphors can mislead. Terms such as "neuron", "attention", "memory" and "learning" mean different things in AI and neuroscience. Treating an artificial unit as a neuron, or an attention head as attention, can import false assumptions.

Hype. Both fields are susceptible to inflated claims, especially when commercial interests are involved. The norms of this book, checking dates, sources and peer-reviewed results, are a defence.

CONNECTIONS FOR A MECHATRONICS STUDENT

If you work at the intersection of robotics and AI, several brain-derived principles are directly usable today: event-based sensing with low latency (13_04); state estimation with Kalman filters, which the brain appears to approximate (13_03); hierarchical control, with fast spinal-like reflexes beneath slower planning, echoing Sherrington's reflex arcs (Chapter 4); reward prediction error learning in reinforcement learning (Chapter 6); and replay buffers for sample-efficient learning (Chapter 9). Equally important is the habit of mind neuroscience teaches: test causal claims with interventions (12_01), be suspicious of single-variable explanations, and remember that real systems are noisy, adaptive and closed-loop.

SUMMARY

Brains still exceed AI in data efficiency, continual learning, energy use, robustness and embodied interaction, and neuroscience offers candidate principles for each, from genomic bottlenecks to replay and local learning rules, though whether to copy principles or mechanisms is debated. AI has given neuroscience task-performing models, benchmarks, analysis tools, precise concepts like distributional reinforcement learning, and fully observable model systems. Both directions are productive, and both require care with metaphors and claims.
